vast increase of the Venetian Commerce, induced pay ments by transfers, or by writing ofilhe SUN to be paid from the account of the payer to the receiver, without the trouBILE Of weighing out goldrand silver Persons thus Interested in
mutual exchanges, obtained charter of incOr pOration for the management OF their joint concerns, and thus produced the bank Of Venice, the first 6anL; euer established an the aoorld, 1t was conducted with such discretion and advantage, that it maintained
its credit unimpeached, through centuries oflev oIution, furnishing the most beneficial facilities to commerce. The example was soon followed, and banks were established in process of time, in all the trading cities of the Mediterranean, with greater or less success,
as they were prudently managed, much as it happens IN our own times, upon W hich the experience of centuries 'shou d not be lost.

New Brick PREss.-We notice, in the machine, invented by John Wnsiow, called the SeyJeedtng Brick Press. The superiority OF this press over others is, that, by laying a Quantity OF impressed brick on a board, the machine removes them one
at time, puts them in the mould, presses them, and places them away, in such manner as entirely to obviate the necessity of handling them in a green state. 1t performs this operation at the rate of fifteen bricks per
minute. Several brick makers of Portland, where the machine is in operation, certify that they have seen many machines for pressing bricks, and have no hesitation in saying that this is far superior to any other kind in nse

PEDLARS. i That" thrre are some honest people in every Calling" is an old adage, and by many believed to be true one nor should we now attempt to dispute its correctness, but for the existence Of a certain worthless,
rowing class Of peopie designated Pedlars, alias travelling merchants.alias venders ofstolen goods. This gang Of spoDgers have no occasion to be honest they not only carry all their worldly effects son their backs, but their characters are there too, nor
does it add great weight to their lug gage. They are without a name. (or if any fictitious one) far away from their acquaintances, so that, should they be detected in any thing dishonest or i'm moral, it would not
have that effect up on their standing in life which It should do. People are not uufrequenily ob!iged to purchase their goods, in order to free themselves Of their company, and instances have been known, where females have been absolutely
frightened into bargain. They'prowl about the country picking up chiidren's ,oppers' to support themselves in idieness and sometimes dissipation. But there are other reasons why this class OF stroll ling knaves should not be encouraged : Every cent paid them
Is dead loss to the town from which il is carried ;there isno more come back to it than thereEs to the specie dollars cent to India il is like throwing money into the sea1t is one of the most
fallacious ideas ev. er admitted into the human ,noddle, that goods are to be bought cheaper of a Pedlar than Of our town and village merchant. There is not single reason for the supposition, Can person who buys of the
wholesale dealer fifty or an hundred dollars worth OF goods, get them cheaper than one who buys thousands? But admitting that some articles could be purchased few cents cheaper ofthese lying vagabond: than Of the regular traders, is it no
pol. icy in me to pay this difference TO m, neighbour, for the chance of again get ting hold Of the money? If L am : halter, shoemaker, or other mechan. ick, is il not to my interest to buy
my dry goods Of the merchant my neigh. bour, TO the end that be may have the wberewi'hal to buy my hats or my shoes? That they do, however, sell any article cheaper than other people, is not true there
is either deficiency in weight or measure, or a, differ ence in quality. 1t is very reasonable to suppose there must be, and in view of this consideration, Pedlars should be classed with Quacks and exhibitors oi learned goats. dancing
bears and pump ing cows. They should not be encOur aged in their idle, dishonest manner o getting living. e
nty of Bachelors. To yoke them whether they will or not tackle them on at all events, Or finger their dollars without saying " your leave" Andi ~, wbep, we look upon the growingl curse Of Old Maids in Cur

Fatal EFFECT OF MATERNAL AM BITsoN.-Maria Theresa believed that her daughters beauty would have proved more powerful over France than her own armies. Like Catharine ii. her enWed cotemporary, she consulted no ties ofnature in the disposal of her children.
When they grew up they became the mere instruments Of her ambition. The fate of one of them will show how their mothers worldliness was rewarded. A leading object Of Maria Theresa's poll cy was the attainment of influence over
Italy: for this purpose she married one ofthe Arcfduchesses 10 the imbecileDuke Of Parma. Her second manuvre was to contrive that Charles Ill. should seek the Archduchess Josepha for his young er son, the King of Naples. When eve ry
thing had been settled, and the cremony, by proxy, had taken place, it was thought proper to sound the princess, as to how far she felt inclined to aid her mothers designs in the Court of Naples, "Scripture says" was
her reply" that when a woman is married, she belongs to the country of her husband" But the "policy of the state J" exclaimed Maria Theresa. "Is that above religion?'cried the princess. This unexpected answer of the Archduchess was so
totally opposite to the views of the Empress, that she was for considerable time undecided whether she would allow her daughter to depart, till, worn out by perplexities, she at last consented, but bade the Archduchess, previous to her setting
off for this much desired country of her new husband, to 60 down to the .tombs, and, in the vaults of her ancestors, offer up to heaven fervent prayer for the depa rted souls of those she was about to
leave. Only few days before that, a Princess had been buried in the vaults--- | think Joseph lis second wife, who had died Of the small pox. The Arch duchess Josepha obeyed her imperial mothers cruel commands, took leave Of
all her friends and relations, as if conscious of the result, caught the same disease, and in few days died.

him were accepted by the state SEN ate. : The naming of Mr.. Hawkins as a "recess appointee" by Governor J. E. Erickson followed the refusal of the senate, by a vote of 27 to II, to confirm the chief
executives nomination of Charles A. Whipple of Broadwater county, a Democrat, to succeed Stewart. Mr.. Hawkins will hold Of flee until after Mr.. Stewards trial which is scheduled to begin before the senate on March 81, and, if the accused
is convicted, until after the election in 1923. The Twentieth legislative session came to an end Saturday, the senate Immediately re-convening as court o+ impeachment. Immediately upo1 taking over the secretary of state'i office, Mr.. Hawkins began an ex haustive

Although the present disaster which has enveloped New England has caused neavy damage to life and property, we'll untold suffering to thousands of people, the northeast is not likely to suffer iously other parts of the country visited by the
cycle of natural tragedies which has made 1927 year long to be remembered. Heavy unreasonable rains, which turned ordinary peaceful rivers into raging torrents carrying death and destruction in their wake, followed by the cold and stormy weather which is
natural to New England at this of the year. Famine and pest ence threatened, but in all probability these add ed horrors will be kept at minimum. New England is compact and is provided with ceent arteries of communication making
relief work much easier than in the Mississippi flood country where wide stretches of land had to be covered by those bringing succor to the unfortunate. Many of these arteries badly damaged, but repair work be rushed. The brunt of
the suffering will not much in the rural sections among the poorer classes in the small towns and cities, with which New England abounds Many of these people will be handicapped for weeks because of damage to the mills and
fact ories in which they work. No call has been sent out to the country at large for relief and it is doubtful if any will be made. New England is hard hit but New England is richer perhaps capita
than any other section of the try and this present blow will not dlshearten those who descended from the hardy pioneers who set led the bleakest part of the country. New England has received, and will appreciate SYM pathy from
the rest of the country, but will undoubt edy be able TO by itself, from its present fortunate condition Sturdy, proud, steadfast New England misunderstood by many other sections of the country, but beautiful place and wonderful people

Mrs. Keyes is going abroad as representative for Good Housekeep. ing and will do a series Of articles under the name Frances Parkinson Reyes. already well known to read ers of the magazine. Her son. Henry Wilder Reyes, jr., will
accompany her as her secretary and they have taken passage on the Majestic. sailing June rs. They will go directly to London to remain two weeks. In August they will spend three weeks in Lausanne and their itinerary for the

carnival. Six teams of stought- hearted north ern dogs-cross breeds and huskieswere entered for the first heat of 40 miles on an Smile course on the Saskatchewan Rive. The second and third heats of 40 miles each are scheduled over
the same course. for Wednesday and Thursday. shorty" Russick. several times winner of the derby. and Emil ST. Goddard were early favorites. Other drivers are Thomas Elvery, Harry Oleansky, Leo St. Goddard and Earl Brydges. Despite the severe weather the
800 mile classic will have none of the hardships of previous years when the event was a 200.miie nonstop affair 100 miles into the wilderness over an unbroken trail along the SaSkatche. wan and 100 miles for the return. The
tive-lap course this year has been packed down by roller, and has a surface as smooth as pavement. The 1926 race was run under similar con ditions, but before that time there were the 200-mile events.

Right Rev. James L. Freeman, Bishop of Washington, will visit st. Paul's Church. on Twenty-thirtl street, tonight at O'Clock and administer the rite of confirmation to class of II candidates, who have been prepared by Rev. A. A. McCallum, rector

The late Bishop Harding was rector of St. Paul's Church before he became Bishop of Washington, and annually returned to his old parish.
by the AhSOttatta IItse' PARIS, January 25.-Eugene Tur. pin noted chemist and inventor of melinnte, died yesterday at Pontoise. near here. Eugene Turpin was born In Paris in l84S. For his discovery of inoffensive colors he was awarded a prize
in 1885. He then began the study of explosives by experimenting with pic rio acid. In addition to melinite, he invented other explosives and also a special Getonator. In 1889. during negotiations with the British gun firm of Armstrong for
the sale Of the English patent Of meiinite, Turpin found that another officer. Ar tillery Capt. Tripone, having acquired the secret of his invention. had sold 1t abroad. This he made public in a book, and Trip0ne was arrested. charged
with treason and convicted. Turpin himself. however. did not es. cape. for he was charged with having made public in his book documents relating to national defense. He was pardoned i'm 1893 and exonerated In 1901 and was attached to
the ministry Of war as artillery expert. Turpin also invented a self propel. ling shell endowned with rotary movement, but it was rejected by French artillery experts as imprac. teal.

Automobile owners were forced to stand in line about two hours today i'm order to obtain their lorig-awaited license plates at the District Building. While the congestion today was not so bad as that of yesterday, when the line of
applicants extended into the street, the rush was sufficient to NIL the ground floor corridors with a seem ingly endless line of weary but good natured men and women. One line today formed near the doorway In the East end
of the build ing. extended down the east corridor along one side of the wall and back again along the other side, and thence through the main front corridor TO the long row of tables midwayof the building. Many Start
Over Again. There were those who thought their quest was over when, after oO minutes of alleged progress. they reached this first row of tables. They were doomed to disappointment, how ever. for these were where the APP plication cards
were to be filled out. Here, also, Is where many persons fell by the wayside, having forgotten such important items as the number Of their engines, the make OF head light lens. etc. The typists insisted on knowing the name
and address of the applicant. the make. style Of body. year and engine number of the car. and the kind of lenses. Those who could not give any or all of these data had to fall out and get them
and then begin the trek all over again. A new line, composed of those with the properly executed blanks In hand, formed at this point and led far around the Fourteenth street cOrridoris to the water registrars Office in the
rear OF the building. The last half of the journey seemed even slower than the first, but every one wealth cred the trip I'm good humor and with out encountering any untoward incl dents. Sight Goal at Last. The first
hour and three-fourths landed the applicants at the rear Of the Fourteenth street corridor, whence they took new tack and started the final stretch. The clatter of rubber stamps then could plainly be heard. The noise served to revive the
tagging spirits of the tlFeu ones. ana dIteT IL seemingly Understandable suspense the ultimate window finally was reached. In the line today were noted bus boys and bus magnates, elevator operators and opponents of other forms of uplift. doctors with
whiskers and patti ents without. clerks, lawyers, chauffeurs and even a mother with an i'm patient 3-year-old at her skirts. All were bent on a common mission and every one took his medicine with the same spirit of optimism.
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. January rs R).-F'looded lowlands. damaged railroad property, ice-laden utility wires and one fatality stood az the toll to-. day of a nine.day stretch of rains and freezing temperatures in Arkansas. Pocahontas in Randolph County, Batesville In Independence
County and Searcy and Judsonia in White County were islands In the midst of expansive lakes caused by overflows. Backwaters from the Little Red River were creeping into the business sec tions of Judsonia. In the northwest. at Bentonville, Mountain
Home and Fayetteville, Ice and sleet hampered telephone and telegraph service, while at Springdale a boy was killed by a live wire which had been snapped by it's burden of Ice. The White, North Fork and Buffalo Rivers were believed
to be falling or at standstill today, but the Black and Current Rivers and the Ouachita were expected to rise further.
PARIS, January 24.-Rumania's erstwhile Crown Prince carol. whose exact status has been somewhat hazy ever since he renounced his royal prerogatives more than a year ago. tx willing TO talk about almost everything but is silent on what Is OF
most interest TO his countrymen and others. Cornered after sitting through a conference on "MOnarchical Institulions on the Balkans" at the SorDonne, he remarked that ne was not going home Just yet" but refused TO discuss reports that his father,
King Ferdinand. was soon to abdicate and that he was to ascend the throne. Leave Politics Alone" Carol admonished correspondents to leave politics alone" or he would run away. This was after he had been asked IL he would return
to Rumania. Then. when questioned about the possibility of a reconciliaton In Italy with his royal wife, Princess Helen, from whom he has been separated for months. he repiled evasively-somethin about the Italian climate In Winter. Inc prince, VINO as
Coral Caratman" has been living In the Paris suburb of Neuilly, confirmed that he had spent the holiday season on the Riviera, having gone there two days before Christmas and returned several days ago. In faultless English he touched on
many topics ranging from foot ball to literature, but as for Balkan and European politics he would say nothing. Hears Professor, Former Tutor. At the conference which Carol at tended the chief speaker was Prof. Nicolas Jorga of the University
of Bucharest. who was tutor to the prince. Carol heard him say that the life of laws is precarious and the powerlessness of kings is increasing" Prof. Jorga is looked upon as a close friend of Carols and IL has
often been remarked that If Carol does assume regal powers. Nicolas Jorga will have an influential positon in the government.

An effort Is being made by the Mexican and United States Govern. ments to arrange what lis known I'm diplomacy as n ''modus vivendi," or temporary arrangement. whereby the rights Of both sides shall not be dis. turbed while an
arbitration tribunal considers the merits Of the case. The United States Government: is willing 10 submit to the General Claims Commission all issues arising out Of the attempt to confiscate Amer. lean oil properties in Mexico, but with the understanding
that no overt act shall be committed in the interim which might prevent the restitution OF property to lawful owners. Two Methods Proposed. Two methods are being suggested to safeguard this phase of the prob lem. One Is that the
Mexican courts shall be asked to grant restraining orders in respect of each individual property and the other that the Mexican government shall give assurance OF Its intention to maintain a status quo while the questions are being decided Already
a number of American companies have applied for and obtained what are known as "amparos," which are equivalent to injunctons. General restraining orders are not customary in Mexican law and an injunction granted. One of the dan gers of this
process so far as American oil companies are concerned is that 1t may involve an examination of proof of titles and in the long series Of changes In government the proof of title Is not always easy to obtain. Commissions
Life Vital. Another problem involved in any temporary arrangement pending arbitration is the question of the duration of the General Claims Commission. BY treaty it's life expires in August of this year unless extended by mutual agreement. Both governments are
dis posed to extend the life of the commits sion for term of years, but 1t has been suggested that the commission might better continue it's work indefi. nitely without any time limit being imposed. The value of the commits
sion Is that 1t has superseded diplomatte channels in the handling of dis putes on property rights and can by reason Of it's experience handle the claims much more expeditiously than the embassies here or in Mexico City. Examination Of
the proceedings OF LIle G)IIHIIiSSiOtl LTuS ItIT TGVcaIio liz fact that It's neutral umpirt>-a M tive Of Holland-as we'll al the Amer lean and Mexican commissioners are basinG their briefs and decisions on the strict letter of international law. This
has led to the belief that If the case were ever submitted to the arbitration of the claims commission the largest question at issue would lie one of fact as to title. Resolution Before Senate. Meanwhile the Senate Is consider.
ing the adoption of resolution favor ing arbitration. This is of little practeal Importance in the present situaton except as n moral support for the legal side of the controversy. Both the Mexican and American govern ments are disposed to
arbitrate. The question Is now to arrange matters in the interim SO that the case can 20 to arbitration. The difficulties of an agreement are as numerous as ever because they involve principles ON which long diplomatic correspond ence has
been conducted for nearly 10 years. II an agreement on detail could be secured in the protocol of submission, there would be little for the arbitral tribunal to decide. Prog ress Is being made, however, and the probabilities are that

written or oral demand is made upon you by the School Tax Collector. Taxes not paid in accordance with the foregoing requirements shall be- come delinquent, and each person shall be subject to a fine of Two Dollars ($2.00). All
persons, firms and corporations employing labor in Alaska shall fur nish to collectors a list of all em- ployes subject to tax, and employers of labor as above set out are author ized by provisions of said Act 10 de-
duct amount of tax from the wages IOf each employ who is subject there to- If any such employers fail to re- port and deduct as herein specified within the period designated for pay ment of said tax, the said

A accident occurred on Sea Gull Island Friday, May 27. when Andrew Jackson, age 19, slipped and fell 30 feet to the rocks below. He had been home a week from Sitka school where he was preparing himself for further
training in the Salvation Army College, with the intention of being an Army officer. With two other boys they made the trip to Sea Gull Island where the accident hap pened Jackson was taken to Hoo- nah and then to
the Juneau govern ment hospital where he died. His skull was badly crushed from the fall and no hope was entertained for his recovery.

are we in business for -' He said the prosperous businessman is the fellow who Is in business, not for himself but for the good of others. There Is not much danger of selishness creeping in if we play he
explained. Make your business ethics and ideals so white that every fellow will feel like a scurvy cur who does any, thing to besmirch or mar the good name of your business or commun- ity. If you build your business
and plan your activities around the word service everything else will take care of itself. AS sooil dS you lower l1O OSe standards and less effectual ideals come in. everything else is all off, and We cant depend on things
you do and you cant depend on things I do.' The minister described the 12 disciples as the first civic club and added "Thc civic club of today is a direct apostolic succession of that little group of men. It
is up to us 10 carry on their work of service to others here in this community. Live so square, play so clean, n'ake your business so white no man will dare besmirch it." No reports were made today on
the Lions frolic. Chairman w. c. French stating that he expected to have complete reports next week. He stated that it was the most suc- cessful affair the club ever had.

European countries informed the Washington government of fears entertained for their nationals in Nicaragua and the president took the view that this aspect Of the question could not be disregarded. Mediation in Nicaragua The president looks upon the question of
mediation in the dispute between the Nicaraguan factions as very largely domestic question in Nicaragua. His chief concern for the United States is that tranquility shall be restored In Nicaragua as soon as possible. As the peace proposals made by
President Diaz of Nicaragua have not come to the White House in any official way, Mir. Coolidge has not undertaken to pass judgment upon them. Congressional discussion of the international situation was reopened simultaneously by critics of the ad- ministration

Judge George NJ. Bourquin, federal Judge of this district, sitting temper arily in the circuit court at Seattle, has attracted much attention at that city as indicated by articles published in the Seattle papers. His personality and his way of
conducting court, both highly distinguished by original characteristics. In an article publish ed by the Seattle Times the following was contained: And when Federal Judge George NJ. Bourquin of Montana, slender, erect, tall, dignified and impressive, takes his regular morning
constitutional through the downtown streets of the city, it recalls to mind the old army Characterization of the north west service men. This is because Judge Bourquin without doubt is one of the most striking figures to be seen on
Seattle streets, as well as being one of the most colorful fig ures on the federal bench in the west. A coal miner, a receiver of "ublic moneys, a state court judge and then a federal judge, Judge Bourquin's his
tory has been one as full of color as his decisions and his actions on the bench. He looks the part. He dresses the part. Always CARRIED in a long tailed Prince Albert Goa, carrying a heavy gold-headed cane and

Minneapolis-(FP) - A movement among stockholders of the defunct Minnesota Daily Star to resist the 25 per cent assessment levied on them by the receiver is under way in Mime apolis and st. Paul. MANY stock holders" says the Minnesota
Union Advocate, "feel that they have little to lose and absolutely refuse to pay a penny into what they consider a huge swindle." Several years ago when the double liability of stockholders was considered by creditors of the defunct Farmer-Labor
daily as a means of raising money, the Mime apolis Central Labor Union took steps to defend the stockholders. There are almost 1000 stockholders, mostly far mers and trade unionists.

Dear Comrades: A month ago we took up Russia in our public school. 1t was for our geography lesson. There are five Pioneers in school. Another comrade and I stood up and told the teacher we could tell the class
something about Russia. / told them why the revolution was started in Russia and what kind of government they have there. My teacher said that the u S. would not need revoluton like that because government is very good to
the people. She also said, 81 don't think we would have such a revolution here. But, if we do, it won't come for another hundred years" Then we began to speak about capital and labor in the U. S. My
teacher said Everyone except the government workers, like the police, paid enough" l said, THAT many people willing to work but they can't find work. Besides, they not paid enough for their work" Ny teacher said, at is lie" Well,
comrades my teacher, that other comrade and had discussion. Finally at the end of our period my teacher said to me, eve didn't study any geography about Russia today only history" The next day when my principal came in my
teacher told her that there were some Bolshevikis in the class The principal called me out and spoke to me. She said that l must love my country and all that bunk. AS | live in the Cooperative House near
Bronx Park she asked all the children living there if they belonged to club and what it was for. Anyway now she leaves US alone. But we have to watch out how we speak in school, If all of you
would think about it you would see the lies that are put into your head in school-RUTH YOUKELSON.
Workers children should be always ready to help the workers when they fight against the bosses. That's what the Young Pioneers said and did when the workers of Passaic striking against their BOSSES They went the picket line they collected
money for food for the strikers and their children They did everything they could to help the workers win Now we hear how the workers children of Gal latin, Pa, have helped the miners who are striking against the Pittsburgh
Coal Company. The bosses had hired some scabs. The workers children decded that the best way to show that they were with the strikers to refuse to go to school with scab children. So this week. as the scab children
walked into school, all the workers children who with the strikers walked out. That's the true Pioneer spirit-always ready to help the workers. Don't you want to be always ready for the of the working class? Join the Young Pioneers
of America and fight together with the workers and their children against the bosses in the school, factory, field or mine Write to us and will tell you how to join.

go into will be the war against you-the class war" Such a formulation can lead to a wrong concepton and more than that it smacks of pacifsm The feminist conception is to fight the imperalist war before and after the

aim of turning the imperalist into civil war, in other words, for the defeat of our own bourgeoisie We are not opposed to all wars. the imperalist efforts to throttle the Soviet Union blossoms into war; we are in favor

BY the Associated Press LONDON, March 26-The wisdom tooth has come in for a sound grill ing at the hands of the Dental Benefit Joint Committee, composed of insurance society representatives and of dentists. The Hearts of Oak Benefit Society
maintains that the wisdom tooth is no good and should be pulled. 1t is non functioning, it is contended, and the society has declined to pay for filings for this "drone" on the ground that as it never does any
work the organication is not obliged to maintain it In the mouth of an insured person. Dentists, however, take an opposite view of the matter. The wisdom tooth should be drilled and filed, but not killed, because 1t is where
1T is for a purpose. they say. The courts may be asked to decide the point.

The high cost of living in cities drove some persons to the farm, and others were induced to take up farm : ing for the satisfaction OF an independent life. Some farmers move to town because they cannot make farming
pay, or are drawn to the city by the lure OF a larger income. Others move because Of better school facilities for their children: others still because of being physically unable to continue farming, and small number because Of f1nancitl
inability to retire. A steady wedding out Of older peo. pie on the farm who are replaced in part at least by men and women in earlier life, was found by the survey. Although the total farm population is reduced
in numbers, the report stated. the result is the development of a more vigorous and efficient agriculture. A detriment, however, is that those who retire take with them to the city a volume of financial wealth and experience the loss

All enlisted men Of the local Guard who aspire to commissions in any branch, and who have reached the eligibility list for promotion by com mission, will be compelled to take the military correspondence course provided for officers and men.
The purpose OF headquarters order is to insure for the commissioned service those men who seriously desire to become military asset, and to do 1t ere willing to put in sufficient time to perfect themselves in the military profession. During
the time that the name of any man remains on the eligibility list for promotion by commission, and while awaiting a vacancy, he will be required to enroll for the correspond ence course of the branch of the service for
which he is found eligible. Each man will be required to com. plete not less than two lessons per month during the time his name appears on the list A man who fails to comply with this order will be
skipped over should O vacancy occur to which he might be entitled, and will not be selected until he complies in full with it's terms. Only a few of the officers of the local guard are taking the mill. tary
courses provided for them, 1t was pointed out, but 1t has been de. ternnined that new material coming In will be compelled to take the courses. First Lieut.. Hugh Everett, tr., was presented with his commission Tues day night by

Capital. Moreover, the series Of changes recently announced concerns us deeply, as many old friends are involved in this game of pussy-wants-acorner, notably Gen. and Mrs. Thomas @. Donaldson, Gen. and Mrs. Abraham G. Lott, Gen. and Mrs. William d.
Conner and Gen. and Mrs. Frank Cocheu. WHILE everybody is delighted w with General Donaldson's promotion to the rank of major general, it has a serious draw back in the fact that it will be followed Immediately by his transfer
to Fort Sam Houston, Tex, to command the Second Division. And the Donaldsons, who are widely known and gen. orally popular, have but recently come back to US after a prolonged absence. They were in the Philippines for a long
time, then at Fort Howard, Md, and it seems but yesterday that the general was ordered to take COM mand of the Sixteenth Brigade, with headquarters in Washing ton. THEIR house in Massachusetts, i Avenue being rented, they settled down
at Stoneleigh Court and now they are unsettled again. packing up for their trek to Texas. They'll be greatly missed. for the interchangeable "Mrs. T. O." loves Washington and Washington loves her. Gen. eral Donaldsons relief is Brig Gen. Herbert
o. williams. who has been on duty at Fort Nc Pherson, Ga. Distress at the loss of Mai. Gen. and Mrs. Hanson Ely, who have gone to Governors Island, Is somewhat mitigated by the fact that Mai. Gen. William D.
Conner is coming from Fort Sam Houston to replace General Ely as commandant Of the Army War College. And General and Mrs. Conner have host of friends here. having repeatedly been on duty in Washington. GENERAL LOTT, also "well VI
and favorably known" to Washington. got his "B. c." through General Donaldson's pro. motion and will replace General Williams at Fort Mcpherson. He has been serving as chief of staff of the Hawaiian Department. General Cocheu, who has been stationed
here from time to time, was not concerned in the promotions which followed the re. tirement of Mai. Gen. Edward M. Lewis. but has been trans ferred to command of the Fourth Coast Artillery District. with headquarters at Fort Mcpherson
and will proceed to his new post on the completion of his present duty at the Coast Artillery School at Fort Monroe. On the retirement of Mai. Gen. William j. Snow, chief of Field Artillery, on December 10, Col. Fred

Various aspects of service to former veterans of the World War given by the American Red Cross were made public in the organizations annual report for the fiscal year ended June 80, announced yesterday. Millions of dollars worth Of Government
insurance was kept in force through efforts Of Red Cross chapters, the report said, particularly during the cam paign prior to the lapsing limit. The sum of $2,930,223 was expended in service during the year for disabled veterans. Prosecution of
claims of veterans is becoming increasingly difficult as the years pass, the report emphasized. recalling that 22,S63 were referred to national headquarters, after direct communication with Government departments had been tried. The in creasing number of death cases COM ing
to the organizations notice was commented on, in calling attention to the point that S55S,681 in Government benefits was secured through activities of the War Service Branch and awards totaling $34.779 in monthly installments of insurance and compen. sation were
secured in addition. III caring 1OE fSlSIdHS III % HOS' pitfalls 16,37S needed and received individual service from Red Cross hospital workers, the report said. Encourage ment of occupational therapy to assist patients in making articles from metal, leather. wood,
by weaving and fashion ing pottery, was an important part of this work. Field directors, the report continued, were on duty at all princi pal stations and hospitals Of the Army and Navy. Supplemental entertain ment and recreation in convalescent
houses and hospital wards were provided. For men of the Army and Navy 07,S32.30 was expended in service. The report found that a monthly average of $4,000 service men, veterans and their families were assisted during the fiscal year. To

Nc LAughlin Is military instructor at the Pennsylvania State College. He il from Michigan and enlisted as private in September 1897. In 1899 he was commissioned second lieutenant Of Infantry and reached the grade Of lieutenant colonel in 1917. During
the World War he commanded the 5th Oregon Infantry and afterward served as a lieutenant colonel of Infantry in the National Army. Col. Mitchell is from Georgia and also began his military career in the ranks. He was appointed a
second lieutenant Of Infantry in 1899 and reached the grade Of lieutenant COLONEL in July, 1920. During the World War he was attached to the National Army in France. He is stationed at Tulsa, Okla. Col. Holcomb is on duty

Settlement has been reached on eight more parcels of land in Rock Creek and Potomac Parkway-property taken over by the Government. The latest accessions are the premises 1911, 1913, 1915, 1917, 1919 and 1921 Twenty-fourth street, and 251S and 2450
P street. There are brick dwell ings now on this property, but they will be allowed to remain until Spring, when they will be razed to make way Tor the park improvements. Cases involving several parcels are still pending, and
the owners do not seem inclined to take what the Gov ernment negotiators call a rea asonable price. If the question of price cannot be satisfactorily adjusted directly between the owners and the Parkway Commission officials. then the matter will
be referred to the Attorney Gen. eral of the United States for the insti. tuition OF condemnation proceedings. Some Of this property is in the tri. angle formed by Rock Creek, M street and Pennsylvania avenue: other lots on the
east bank of Rock Creek be. tween Pennsylvania avenue and L street and several other pieces on the south side Of P street.

The neglect tax is the biggest single destroyer of our wealth. The nations big bill, losses caused by insect pests, is about $1,3OO,OO0,0OO a year. We hear much of the boil weevil, Japanese beetle and corn borer, and the govern
ment spends large sums to help farm ers combat these pests. Yet we hear little of neglect losses, which are greater than insect losses. Insects destroy potential wealth. Neglect destroys invested capital and reduces the interest earned by money invested
in property. The neglect tax is more than douBILE the fire loss, about which so much is written. This matter Of deprecialton is not given the dramatic at tention which is accorded the fire loss because it's slow accumulation leads
people to overlook it. Neglect taxes reach $1,419,6O0,OO0 a year. OF our standing property worth approximately SOL, 4O0,0OO,O00, only about 80 per cent is adequately protected, the balance is deteriorating at the rate Of about per cent year.
If certain family pays a sixth of its income for rent, it may be able to devote one-fourth or more to buying and maintaining house, for the amount thus used may include both rent and savings. Rent, or pay ments
on home, may require any where from one-eighth to one-third of the family income, depending on the special circumstances in each case. In addition to interest payments and installments on the principal of a loan, allowance must be made for
renewals and repairs. taxes, special assessments, insurance, water tax and various accessories and improve ments. Families accustomed to living in apartments sometimes fail to al low for the cost of fuel for heating purposes.

Country road lighting is getting a tryout in this country. A nine-mile section of the highway between Can andaigua and East Bloomfield, N. Y, for the past three months has been Illuminated by electric lamps at in tervals of 200
and 250 feet. Automobile clubs, chambers of commerce, local oranges and other such organic atoms are backing the plan because drivers see their routes so much more readily and because pedestrians get much more protection along high way.

Following the example Of the United States In setting aside the District Of Columbia, the Australian parliament carved out of the state Of New South Wales q federal district 1000 miles square which Is to be governed by a commission.
There is one important difference between the District of Columbia and the District of Can berra. In the latter there can be no freeholding of property. The commits sion leases land to private individuals, but does not sell it. In
this way it Is enabled to keep its hand on the develOpment Of the property. And this is where the city planner receives his boon. He is able to say that this part of the city shall be an industrial
district, and 1t Is an indus trial district; he says that another section shall be a fine residence dis trict, and it is that way. Another area he designates as district for moderate priced homes. And so on. He zones
the city, and nothing can be put into the respective zones that Is not authorized, and which is not COM patible with the surroundings. Canberra is now in the process of construction. During the next quarter of century it is
expected to become one of the greatest cities in Aus tralia. City planners throughout the world will watch the experiment OF thus creating what might be termed a custom-made city, and will learn much from this great enterprise, the first

Log-book is the book In which the master of a ship enters each day a brief but exact account of all the events Of that day, the miles made by that days run of the ship, an account of the
weather, and the names Of vessells sighted or spoken when names can be obtained. The log is the Off. cial record of the voyage.

Hartford, July 22.-F-Automo- bile accidents in the state during the week which ended July 16 showed an unusually large increase over the number during the corresponding week of 1926, according to the week ly accident report issued today by the
department of motor vehicles. There were 527 crashes as compar- ed with 3S0 a year ago. Two accidents on the Milford turnpike. each of which killed two persons, brought the total number of fatalities to six. Last year there were
three fatal accidents during the corresponding week. Those killed last week and the places where the accidents occurred: Darien, Richard Riis; Pawcatuck, Mary Sullivan; Milford, John Shreve and Adele Shreve; Orange, Thomas King and Louise King. Of the total number
of accidents. 276 were in the fourteen cities for which detailed reports are given as compared with 214 last year. New Haven had as many accidents as Hartford, each city reporting 49. while there were 48 in Bridgeport. Totals for
the other cities were as follows; Waterbury 35; New Brit ain 20 Stamford 14; Meriden 12: Greenwich 10: New London g; South Norwaik g; Danbury 8; Norwich z: Winsted 1; Middletown ?.
Geneva, July 22 R-The Ameri- can delegation to the tripartite naval conference remains adamant in up- holding the right to build cruisers armed with eight-inch guns, accord ing to information in reliable quar- ters here today. Furthermore, it is understood
that in taking this stand in defense of American naval requirements the delegates advocate cruisers large enough to carry a battery of six S-inch guns instead of merely one or two. Naval experts here estimate that a cruiser carrying six
8-inch guns should have a displacement of $500 tons British delegates have been in aisting on limiting secondary cruis- CTS of 6,000 tons with no guns larg- CT than six-inch caliber. Should the British delegates return from their present visit
to London with a man. date from their government to up- hold this demand, it is feared in some conference circles that definite breaking off of negotiations might ensue. Belief is expressed here that the British government has been fore
warned that the American delegates are determined, whatever may be the outcome, to insist upon the lib- erty 10 construct whatever type of cruiser the United States may deem essential for her naval needs.

'equipment and ac- cessories' in the June department bulletin. All cars, except those with spe- cial permit, must be equipped with headlight devices on the approved list the bulletin says. "Twenty- one candle power is the maximum for any electric
lamp or bulb in such devices" The use of accessory lighting ap- pliances in combination with ap- proved devices is discouraged. be- cause it is believed that there are enough efficient approved devices to meet all needs if they are
properly used. The present attitude of the department. however, is that access sorry devices may be used by motor iStS upon their own responsibility, provided they do not conflict with the legal requirements. "Connecticut has no approved list of tail
and signal lights" the bullc- tin continues. but any such light which complies with the Massa : chusetts requirements will be satis- factory here. It is required that when tail lights are lighted, they shall, in addition to showing red
to the rear, also sufficiently illuminate rear number plates with a white light to make them legible at dis tance of 50 feet. Number plates, both front and rear, must be kept clean, unohscured by any other part of the
equipment and should be fastened to the vehicle in such q way as not to swing and so that the lower edges of the plates shall be at least 14 inches from the ground"

Oklahoma City, Okla, July 22 R With daily output of nearly half million barrels of oil--slightly less than one-fifth of the national total threatening an already weakened crude market, operators in the com paratively new greater Seminole field today faced
an ultmatum from the state corporation commission 10 cease completions in the larger pools. The commission intervened in the curtailment program, started by leading operators at meeting in New York last spring in an effort 10 bolster crude prices, when
it issued a temporary restraining order last night prohibiting drilling in or shooting wells in certain sections of the field. The commission is en- powered to act in cases involving petroleum conservation. The order was made returnable August 5, when
operators will be invited to attend a hearing in an effort to break the deadlock on development of the Seminole Field. Ray NJ. Collins appointed last May as umpire to supervise the curtail ment project recommended comple ton of the
450 wells then being drilled, but advocated limitation of production on scale intended to balance the output from the hold ings of the various companies. Collins yesterday appealed to the corporation commission to exercise It's auth ority. he declared that
unless some action was taken, further re- auctions of from 25 to 50 cents a barrel would result. Prices yesterday ranged from s1.22 to s1.0 a barrel.

Governor Young of California gives seven reasons for pardoning Charlotte Anita Whitney, and they are all good. Boiled down, however, they simply mean that in the Governor S opinion Miss Whitney is not a GRIM inal and would never have
been tried, much less convicted, but for abnormal conditions incident to the war. 1t is impossible to read this brief but punchful statement without gaining the impression that he thinks the anti-syndicalism law, under which Miss Whitney was convicted, should
be laid on the shelf. This country passed lot of fool ish laws and did lot of foolish things during the World War. Miss Whitney's convection and pardon is just an illustration of the wild conclusions to which We rushed
in our excitement and of the revision of opinion that now becomes necessary. We even insisted that sauerkraut be called liberty cabbage, as though that had anything to do with beat ing the kaiser.

Ignis fatuuS, or will-o- the-wiSp, - both mystery and paradox. For centuries its name has been house, hold word; or rather its names, for it bears at least fifty in English and a great many in other languages. J.. Though
so often reported over a great part of the world it has never been the subject of thorough scientifc investigation. Nobody has ever studied its light with the spec troscope, for example. Chemists have sometimes tried to reproduce the phenomenon,
but the chemical explanations of it that have APP peared in reference books down to a recent date are quite untenaole. The tendency nowadays Is to regard most of the appearances described as willo'-t he-wisp as due to the phenomenon
of lunlinescence. This phenomenon is exhibited by many species of plants and animals; especially by fungi In Europe there are certain kinds of gnat that become luminous through disease. Little swarins of these dancing creatures have PROBABLY oIJeN peen described
as ignis fatuus, The luninescence of decaying wood. known as fox fire" may explain other cases. This phenomenon is very common in the Dismal Swamp and is fairly well known elsewhere. Barn owls are said to become luminous at times
through rubbing their feathers against such wood in emerging from their holes. One authority believes that swarns of luminous bacteria are sometimes carried up from marshes by bubbles of rising gas. Will-o'-t he-visp though it nas nqm obvious connection with
weather, 4 generally classed as a meteorological phenomenon. Formerly 1T wss dis cussed in most treaties on meteorol~ ogy. but it is completely ignored in nearly all the recent works on this subject. All rights reserved by Science Service. Inc

Nan Hartley posed for living. She hadn't any particular talent, ana mel beauty was such a decided asset that at the suggestion of a friend she hao commercialzed it. Nan was very beautiful. She had tiny face that looked as
If it had been carved out OF a cameo. Her nose was small and her lovely, wide mouth curved over perfect teeth. Her eyes were blue-violet blue-and her dark ahair, short, of course, waved back from a broad, white forehead.
She had the kind of beauty that artists went mad over, so that she seldom had any trouble getting work. She posed for magazine covers. H. Illustrations of different kinds, com mercial art and anything she could get. 1t wasn't
easy work, because 1t meant holding a pose that was often very difficult. Sometimes the artist would forget, too. Absorbed in his work. he would neglect TO say: Don't you want to rest, Miss Hart ley?" Nan could never bear
to interrupt an artist, so she would grit her teeth and hold on for dear life. Sometimes, when she at last relaxed, her tortured muscles would ache like a toothache. once when she had been crouching on the floor in
an unnatural pose she had toppled over, and the sudden, sharp agony OF relaxation had made her burst into hysterical tears. A long list of artists had her name and address, and would call her on the telephone when they
needed her type. She averaged about $40 a week, al though there were weeks when she made more. Nan had gone into the work of pos ing with some dread. She had read magazine stories about the things that went
on in artists studios, and had formed her ideas accordingly. She had visions of tiger-skin rugs hanging from balconies and of the artists themselves working in velvet dressing gowns and trying to make love to her. She had started out
in fear and trembling, going from studio to studio; but, for the most part, she had found her fears groundless. OF course, she had had one or two unpleasant expert ances, but she might have had those In any business
Office. In almost every case the artist, usually in a smock or a WORKOUT dress. ing gown, worked in a big. bare studio. Canvasses Uttered the walls They were piled everywhere. The harsh, searching light from huge north skylight filled
the room. The same formula was repeated again and again. Nan would say, shyly: 81 am look. ing for work" And the artist, usually in the midst of some creative work, and, for that reason, busy and distracted, would stop
because of her amazing beauty. At first she was embarra ssed at the way they stared at her; but later she realized that there was nothing per sonal about it. They stared at her critically because her features were so
fiawless Already they were fitting her into some possible creation. They all said the same thing, too:
would you mind taking off your hat, so that l can see the shape or your head?" Nan was beautiful with hat, but without one, and her broad forehead. with it's widows peak showing, she , was breath-taking. Usually the
artist would simply stare at her loneliness. Then he would invariably say: "Of course, l can use YOU" and he would whip out a little black note book and take here telephone number. Nan lived in a cheap little apart
ment on the outskirts Of Greenwich Village. She cooked her breakfasts and most Of her dinners on a two burner gas stove. What pleasure she had came from outside. through peopie who were kind to her; and there were quite
a few Of these. One afternoon, when she had been | posing for Duncan Malcolm, very | charming woman had dropped in. She, too, exclaimed at Mans ectraorbinary beauty, and she sat and watched the giru pose, while she smoked
cigarette after cigarette. When Nan finished, she sugfigested taking her home in a taxi. You look tired" friendship developed between herself and Helen Sheridan, who had plenty of money and was bored with the people in her own set. SO
that, on occasions, Nan was in vited here and there. She couldn't afford to spend much money on clothes: but somehow it didn't seem to matter, and it was at a dinner given by Helen Sheridan that she met Martin
Lee. Nan wasn't stupid; she wasn't the beautiful and dumb type at all. She could talk intellgently on most subjects, but Martin Lee didn't care whether she talked or not. He didn't see her until they were all seated at
| the table, and then he opened his mouth and quickly closed it again. Across the table he saw the most | incredibly beautiful girl he had ever | beheld in his life. She looked like a | Madonna. So
few women could wear | their hair like that: it required a | hawless profile. Utterly obliviOus to | the woman who was his dinner part ner, he stared at Nan across Tiffany | bowl filled with yellow tea roses
until | his eyes drew her and she looked at him. only to flush scarlet and turn away. / Alter UlIlIlPF ne WAS pIeSeIltcu W | her, and they sat and talked for a | time. She liked him at
once. He was | about 40, with hair that was already CRAVING at the temples. His eyes We're very deeply set under heavy | brows. He looked clever. Later | Helen told Nan that he was one of the |
biggest corporation lawyers in the | country. She looked at Nan closely as she vouchsafed this information; but, al though the girl seemed interested, she wasn't unduly impressed. | Helen and Nan had often talked | about such things as
love and ronance and marriage, and Helen knew | Mans ideas in a general way. She | believed absolutely in love. She could no more bring herself to like a man because he had money than she could throw herself
into the river. But Helen couldn't help thinking, as she talked to Nan, that it would be a marvellous thing if the girl could fall in love with Martin Lee. He was | rich, good-looking and he had power. |
He was director in one of the big gest railroads in the country. Nan had swept him off his feet, too. But beyond a certain point Helen did not dare to go with Nan. The girl had reticences. When she
felt that she was being pumped for information OF any kind she would shut up like a little clam. That enchanting face of hers would assume an almost naughty | look. Yes, Nan liked Martin Lee; but she knew at
once, as most girls do, that she could never love him. And when she discovered, as she did almost al once. that he was in love with her she was disturbed by it. Copyright. 1927 Continued in tomorrow's Starr

BIZ United Press CAPETOWN, South Africa, March 5.-Unconfirmed wireless reports from Madagascar today said there had been several hundred casualties during cyclone there. The first report of the disaster came from Maui ritius. 1t said five hundred persons had been
killed or injured and that the town of Tamataye, on the east coast Of Madagascar, had been dew astated by the cyclone Of Tuesday. A subsequent, and so far uncon firmed, wireless message from NADIA gascar said several hundred persons
had been killed. The French steamers Vile DE Marseilles and Catinat were reported to have been driven ashore. The Union Castle steamer Gaika wire lessed that she. had encountered terrific storm.
f. M. Washington, Cleveland, Ohio, will think twice before he again plays the good Samaritan and shares his bed with a stranger. Friday night he met a neatly dressed though shabby young man who spun him a tale of woe,
he told police. Washing ton, taking pity on the youth. offered to share his hotel room with him and they retired together. An hour later Wash ington, was awakened by the house detective. The door of his room was open,
the youth was gone. and with him $125 which had a short time before had nestled in Washington's wallet.

BY OLIVE ROBERTS BARTON We are told that many of the undesirable characteristics a child may develop in youth or later years are the result of too close contact with its mother. just when a child is old enough to
spend part of his time away from his mother, or with whom, depends upon circumstances; the child's physical condition, for instance, the community in which he lives, his ability to look out for himself, and other things as well. However
1t happened in the old days that the wise gentlemen who started public schools picked on the age of 6 to separate Johnny from the maternal apron st, lg. and kept him away from her the biggest part of every
day for five days week for nine or ten months a year, cannot say. But they decreed better than they lnew. For, all things being equal, the present-day character special lists would do exactly the same thing, it seems. Kindergarten
may be regarded perhaps in a different light. Children start to kindergarten at 4 and begin then to learn the organized play that prepares the mind for further cultivation when he reaches school age. The best thing that can happen
to a child is the law that takes him away from his mother for several hours a day at 6 years Of age. He begins to be a unit in the world of men. There is no one to back
him. He must learn to depend on him self. His trips to and from school may be punctuated with an occassional battle, but battles at 6 and battles at go are not so different. He must learn to win at
6 if he is to win later. His little backbone must stiffen some time. Competition, they say, IS the life of trade. Competition likewise is the life of the boy and he cannot start too soon. They learn other things,
too. They learn justice to others, they learn to be good losers, they learn to admire winner. All these things amount to as much or more than the knowledge gained from books. And they are things that his mother cannot

BY MRS. WALTER FERGUSON There are certain things that women- cannot do alone. For no matter how we may talk about our equal ity, our ingenuity and our daring, men will always be the Adventures OF the race. Theirs is
the task of going first into the earth, first into the sea and first into the air. They discovered the continents, found new worlds in the heavens, conquered the barren wastes and made the deserts blossom. No matter how we
may yearn, we cannot compete with them in exploration. Miss Doran, the Inflated girl who was lost with one of the ships in the race to Hawaii, though the world admired her courage, did not contribute one thing TO the
science of aviation. She went to her death unne cessarily- tragic figure Of youth, whose passing was attended by the notice of all nations, but who might have lived for many years and accomplished much good in a field more
fitted for the feminine. Made Only Stir And the Princess LowensteinWertheim, though we must admire the spirit of her 63-year-old soul, created nothing but monetary stir by her attempted flight across the Atlantic. Women may be just as intelligent, and
just as courageous, but it was meant for men to accomplish the spectacular. Our bravery must be exhibited in more quiet, if no less important ways. We can bear more pain, stand more sorrow, and endure more abuse than men.
But we are neither strong enough nor wise enough to build airplanes and pilot them alone across the seas; we cannot go into the jungle and conquer nature there; we cannot cope with the arctic regions and survive. Woman's Work
For we have other work to do. If some woman had not been willing to bear child, had not been willing to exercise the patience of mother hood, had not possessed that great est bravery Of all, that of the
spirit, so that she was willing to give up her son for great deeds, Lindbergh might never have made his heroic gesture of defiance to the great waters, In the biggest things women can only follow in the footsteps of
the intrepid male. Why, therefore, are we not content to exhibit our courage, our patience and our endurance in the lowlier places where they may accomplish deeds not so startling, but fully as great as those of men?

per annum, which will in clude board, room, tuition and al necessary expenses except personal Attractive Buildings The auditorium will be of Spanish renaissance design with red tiled roof and white walls, flreproof, YET graceful in its lines. Bedrooms will
be large, cool and roomy; there viii be showers and fudge kitchens, special dining rooms for the young men callers" special bedrooms folvisiting parents, "a browsing room where a girl may read and loaf and invite her soul--every conceivable appliance
for physical training These are some Of the advantage; Scripps College will offer the young woman of today. Every student will be required tc live in the dormitory. There will be no sororities and every endeavoi will be made to
develop spirit Of genuine democracy among the girls who are privileged to attend. More than all else, individual effort will be stressed-the call of the creative spirit. No definite PLANS as TO detailN Of curricula have as yet been worked
out, but Scripps College will stress the fundamentals in liberal arts the first two years, and preparation FOL life in the upper class years.

Dy C La isSTsSdr CAL, Sept. 49, Under the mighty shadow Of snow capped MT. San Antonio, upon a slightly plateau at the north of Pomona College campus, is rising right now the first unit Of the Scripps College for
Women. 1t is more than seventy years since Mills College for girls was founded in the hills back of Oak land, and in all this time no other institution Of higher learning for women has been projected upon the Pacific
coast. " But now, barring the unforeseen, the dream Of a great college for women in Southern California is coming true. Built Like Oxford 1t is significant of the unique plan of Scripps College that its first building will be
the dormitory for the freshman class for from the very first the plan Of this college has been different. Conceived by a great woman Scripps College is to be the second unit in an unique group in America, built after
the Oxford plan, group of small colleges, where individual training may be given, yet where all the advantages of great university may be realized, The first unit of what is now known as "Claremont Colleges" is Pomona College, a co-educational
institution of distinction, now forty years old, and ranking in equipment with the best institutions of similar size in the country, and in scholar ship with. the highest in the land. Limiting its student body to 300, Pomona College enjoys
continual ly frightening waiting list of eligibles, eager to meet the ever in creasing demands for higher scholarship, necessary for admission. Hopes to Give ALI Scripps College for Women owes its existence to the brain and gen. crosby of Ellen
Browning Scripps, elder sister of the late Edward w, Scripps, founder of what is today the Scripps- Howard League OF newspapers, who now, in her ninety first year, lives and plans and gives not alone Of her income but of

boys seemed to enjoy it equally as we'll. To make her subject as interest ing as possible she changed the various ways of attaining health into jewels. She called the girls diamonds. some bright and some dull She explain to
the dull ones how to become clear and sparkling, and to the bright ones how to keep their luster. ITO do this is to keep morally and physically clean" she said land it is so easy. There is no reason
why you should not all be clear and crystal gems" Her talk was tinted with humor, which of course captured ~ of the pupils when she had concluded she received applause.

When | first started the study of Geography | did not like it because il seemed dull, dry and difficult to learn. l have gained q lot of pleasure from the prepare ton of my LESSONS this year. ] have
learned the odd habits of other people, the way they live and what they wear. We have written to the Chamber of Com ferce in different cities for literature on their activities, and they have been kind enough to send
what they had. II has been a real pleasure to find pictures and items bearing on our lessons, and to bring them to class. The pictures taken from newspapers and magazines ment more to us when we know some thing
of the people. We have travelled on imaginary Journeys throughout Asia and find that many useful things in our homes come from these far off countries Now we are in the sunny land of Central America. While we SILVER with
cold, it is a pleasure to think of the flowers, shrubbery and wonderful trees that give this mountainous land such beautiful scenery We are hoping the masses of people living in this country so near us will become better educated,
Then they can have peace and enjoy the things nature has given them. BY IRMA LEWIS-Seventh Grade, Park avenue school.

A number of residents living on Brooklawn street who are not in- clined to avail themselves of the privilege of free mail delivery will be required to call at the post office for their mail in the near future, If
developments in the mail situation in that locality today are any criterion. One other resident on the street last evening communicated with Postmaster H. E. Erwin. stating that now that the street has been given the privilege Of free mail
delivery he Is anxious to have the service and is willing to comply with regulations. He was told that as long as only one or two residents on the street con- ply with the regulations calling for mail receptacles. at
the homes' no mail will be delivered there. This man stated, as did woman the night before, that he would use what influence he had with his neighbors to get mall re ceptacles installed, He was told that the post

The Northern Arizona Teachers college at Flagstaff reopened De, cenlber 2S for the winter quarter with an increase fn' attendance tha; surpasses that of any former year The college has been graduating students four times a yehr. This system has
been in vogue for the past year and, while it may appear to be burdensome project on the part of the administration, 1t is a great service as an opportunity for county s&3orintendents, principals and boards of trustees to be
able to FIJI vacancies with very little diff Guilty. There mas beent some talk, how eyer. of decreasing the number of graduation exercises, holding them in June and at the end of the sum, mer session in August. Those stu
dents who are graduated in JAM uary and in March would return for the exercises in June This, it is said will create a better and finer spirit among the student body and The alumni.

Recent magazine and newspaper articles throughout the country have been bringing to the attention of the public ut large the unusual advantages presented by the Capital City. There is probably no city in the United States whose growth has been
as carefully planned and guarded as has WashingtonS. From it's beautiful buildings to it's less pretentious residential districts all go toward making a complete one ness. A very concise realization of what Washington eventually will be can be gotten by
visiting the National Museum, where a model in relief depicts Washington as il was laid out by the Mcmillan Commission. This plan for future Washington was de signed to meet the needs for many years to come, further developing the
excellent LEnfant plan Federal Building Plans The S50.OO0.O00 appropriation for the building of Government buildings and the development Of the Mall brings us a few steps nearer to our goal. Washington is. without doubt. 4 city offering some Of the
greatest adj Nantages 0btainable in the world. Educational institutions, art museums, Libraries, splendid parks-all go toward making up an ideal city. A full appreciation of Washington can be readily gained by comparing advantageS here with those in other cities. The
many parks in and about Wash 1ngton take from Washington streets much of that which is oppressive in the unusually large cities. Where, if YOU please, is there another city that within one square of the busiest cor rers is
Il park that is equal to our Farragut. Lafayette and Mcpherson Squares or Potomac Park? All of the quiet that could be gained in the most remote spot in the country can be DELIGHTFULLY."- enjoyed in these down town Ravens.
Termed City of Homes. Washington has been well termed the city of homes. Construction and development of land in and about Washington has been made only with the beauty of the city in mind. Here one will find the finest
type of archilecture, plus marked modern home construction and appointment, as we'll as splendid living conditions. We hear of a slump in real estate values; we hear of an overbuilt mar ket; we hear of a possible drop in prices.
There is no basic information on which to ground this rumor, but if any of these conditions Go exist they will affect only those parts of Wash lngton that have been badly developed, but not the more carefully planned and
executed subdivisions. A standard product. standard in vestment, always remains standard" Those operators who are building Washington in accordance with the original splendid ideals brought forth by George Washington and L'Enfant, and further developed by the McMi1Ian Commission, cannot fail
in their projects, but can do and have already done much to make Washington worthy of its importance-the Capital City of the United States
